This was the first mission undertaken to Austria for this purpose. It formed part of a wider series of missions to all Member States evaluating control systems and operational standards in this sector. /(*$/ %$6( The mission was carried out under the general provisions of Community legislation and, in particular: · Council Directive 80/217/EEC1 of 22 January 1980 introducing Community measures for the control of classical swine fever. 1 Official Journal L 047, 21/02/1980 p. 0011 - 0023 4 · Council Directive 90/423/EEC2 of 26 June 1990 amending Directive 85/511/EEC3 of 18 November 1985, introducing Community measures for the control of FMD. · Commission Decision 91/42/EEC4 of 8 January 1991 laying down the criteria to be applied when drawing up contingency plans for the control of FMD, in application of Article 5 of Council Directive 90/423/EEC5. · Commission Decision 98/139/EC6 of 4 February 1998 laying down certain detailed rules concerning on-the-spot checks carried out in the veterinary field by Commission experts in Member States. %$&.*5281' +LVWRU\ The FMD and CSF non-vaccination policy adopted by the EU together with increasing trade, reduction in border controls and the illegal movements of animals have increased the risks of an outbreak and have highlighted the importance of developing suitable contingency plans. As a consequence, Community legislation requirements have been put in place and each Member State is required to draw up a contingency plan and a manual of operations for the two diseases. Between 1973 and 1975 a number of outbreaks of FMD were recorded in Austria; the isolates were of type O and C. The last two outbreaks were declared in 1981 in Lower Austria. The first involved a herd of five pigs and the second a herd with 37 cattle. The virus isolated in the two outbreaks was type O. The source was not identified but an illegal import or swill feeding were suspected. CSF was first reported in Austria in 1921. A number of outbreaks were recorded between 1990 and 1994 and one in 1995 in Lower Austria in a large modern farm, not involved in swill feeding or import. Two outbreaks of CSF in wild boar were declared in July 1996 also in Lower Austria, close to the border with the Republic of Slovakia. If provinces (%XQGHVOlQGHU) fail to comply they may be taken to the Constitutional Court. The Federal Veterinary administration is divided into six departments: meat hygiene, animal health and disease eradication, imports from third countries, control of drugs, feed control and intra-Community trade. There are a total of 14 veterinarians employed in these six departments. All the aspects related to the elaboration and implementation of the contingency plans are covered by the animal health and disease eradication department. This department is further divided into two sections: the first budget and laboratories and the second list A diseases. In each of the provinces there is a Director who is responsible for the implementation and co-ordination of the measures on animal and public health in all the administrative districts of the province. At provincial level the total number of official veterinarians is 74 and at district level 134 (1-3 veterinarians per district according to the size and animal population). Under the Austrian Animal Health Act, practitioners may be hired to assist official veterinarians during emergencies or vaccination campaigns where insufficient permanent staff is available. If they are involved in the eradication of a notifiable disease, they cannot practise at the same time. The Federal Government is in charge of the payment for the practitioners recruited. In Styria (Steiermark) there is a policy of employing practitioners as part time official veterinarians for 20% of their time. This temporary staff is mainly used for meat inspection and in the screening for diseases such as tuberculosis, brucellosis and leucosis. The provincial governor, as the principal authority in the province, plays an important role in case of an outbreak. His/her tasks are related to crisis management, public information and organising assistance. There is no guarantee in law that compensation to farmers would be paid within sixty days of animals being slaughtered, as proposed in the Commission Guidelines on Contingency Plans. The CA declared that the compensation to farmers is made between 3 to 6 months after the slaughter of animals. Valuation is made by an "appraisal commission" consisting of the official veterinarian, two experts from the locality plus a practitioner of the farmer's choice. This applies to cattle and breeding pigs only. The price of piglets and fattening pigs (and poultry) are determined by a scale based on the market. There is no National Insurance scheme for farmers but some provincial governments have special funds to cover non-notifiable animal diseases. &KDLQ RI FRPPDQG DQG 1'&& The Federal Chancellor is responsible for all legislation regarding FMD and CSF. The CVO is responsible for the implementation of the legislation, for all national measures regarding the elimination of the diseases, for the operation of the NDCC and for the co-ordination, if an outbreak crosses provincial boundaries, of the activities of the provincial authorities concerned. The provincial veterinary authorities are responsible for the establishment of the LDCCs and the DDCCs and for the implementation of the eradication and control measures at provincial (%XQGHVOlQGHU) and administrative district level (9HUZDOWXQJVEH]LUNH). The chain of command, and the connections that should be established between the three different levels, is well-defined and there is constant contact between them. The tasks of the NDCC are laid down in the plans and include contacts with: NRL, LDCCs, press and other media and the Federal Ministries for Land and Forestry, Foreign Affairs and Finance. Contacts are also established with the heads of the Provincial Government of the Bundesländer, the Veterinary University, and the Federal Chambers of veterinarians and economists. The NDCC is also in charge of reporting disease outbreaks to the Commission, Member States, international organisations and neighbouring third countries. Further tasks include the establishment of vaccination areas and the distribution of vaccine if emergency vaccination is considered. Additional staff may be recruited by the NDCC when the number of official veterinarians is considered to be insufficient to carry out all the necessary measures. 9 The amendments and the recommendations introduced into the contingency plans and/or in the manual of operations are also under the responsibility of the NDCC. No specific facility in the headquarters of the Federal Veterinary Services has been designated as the NDCC and no telephone or fax lines are available exclusively for emergencies. The list of official veterinarians, organisations and people to be contacted was available. At present, there is no direct computerised access to the bovine identification database (AMA) and the information requested by the Federal Veterinary Services is sent out from the AMA by e-mail. The AMA is however only accessible for four and a half days per week. It was indicated by the CA, that direct computer access to AMA would be established in the next six months. In order to make decisions on disease control the NDCC relies on information received from the LDCCs. There is considerable variation in the data registration systems used by the nine provinces. In five of them the GIS is in place. However, in Upper Austria and Lower Austria, where the livestock population is highest, the registration system is not tied in to a mapping programme. recommendations.text: The CCA's strategy on animal welfare in dairy farms is a part of the general umbrella of the Animal Welfare Plan 2014-2018. This plan includes extending the work of the Animal health Service (Österreichischer Tiergesundheitsdienst ­ TGD) to identify practical animal-based indicators for measuring animal welfare.

The TGD is composed of representatives of the Chambers of Veterinary Surgeons, of Agriculture, of Commerce, and of Labour, and representatives from the Federal Ministry for Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water Management. Its main objective of the TGD is to minimise the use of medicinal products and improve animal health. A TGD representative indicated that concerning dairy farming: · 60% of Austrian dairy farms are members of the TGD. Farms that are members must have a contract with a private veterinarian who has to carry out an annual farm evaluation on medicinal use, animal health and welfare; · membership to the TGD is a requirement to become a member of the Austrian Agriculture Organisation's (AgraMarkt Austria) quality assurance scheme 'QS Cow' (QS Kuh). The majority of dairy farmers that are members of the TGD are members of this scheme; · members of the TGD have access to free milk testing (including for somatic cell count); · information collected from the dairy farms is stored in the TGD database and made available to the competent authority; · the TDG organises courses and events together with the Chamber of Agriculture (see also Paragraph 4); · the farmers met by the audit team highly valued the activities carried out by the TGD.

AgraMarkt Austria's quality assurance scheme 'QS Cow' is 50% EU-funded and 50% funded by the Federal State and the provinces. This assurance scheme includes: 5 · one control on each farm at least every four years. If the check detects an animal welfare problem the frequency is increased to an annual basis; · collection of milk samples from members nine to ten times a year. The scheme sends the results of these samples back to the farmers. They include a comparison of each of their animals' performance against the national average. These results are also communicated to, and stored by, the TGD; · an early warning system against mastitis. Farmers are notified when the somatic cell count of a milk sample exceeds 100,000 or is more than twice the count of the previous sample. This enables the farmer to assess the cow and carry out further tests, if necessary, to investigate for the presence of mastitis.

All farmers have to be members of the Chamber of Agriculture. Funding for the Chamber of Agriculture originates mainly from membership fees according to farm size. Provincial administrations contribute to the Chamber's funding. The roles of the Chamber of Agriculture include: · providing information to farmers, including on animal welfare issues. The Chamber of Agriculture publishes and distributes agricultural journals to its members (one national and another different for each province). It also organises courses and seminars. Some of these events are organised with the TGD, e.g. on topics such as fertility, udder health, and interpretation of milk testing reports; · an advisory service covering udder health, milk quality, inspection of milking equipment (if high cell counts have been detected), construction of new stalls or modernisation of stalls (in close collaboration with the TGD) and organic production. Some of the advisory activities incur an additional cost.

The umbrella organisation for cattle breeding in Austria is the Association of Austrian Cattle Breeders (Zentrale Arbeitsgemeinschaft österreichischer Rinderzüchter) which encompasses the Chamber of Agriculture, breeding organisations and artificial insemination centres. A subsidiary of this organisation manages the breed indexes for the main dairy breeds kept in Austria. The estimation of the breeding value is carried out in conjunction with German breeding organisations. The breed indexes include values for: somatic cell count, calving, fertility and longevity.

The main focus of dairy farm research carried out in Austria is on the production of food from healthy animals, sustainability and efficiency of resources but also on maintaining competitiveness using high-level technology. There are several research projects with impact on animal welfare, e.g.: · Advancement of Dairying in Austria (K-Projekt ADDA), supported by the Federal government and the provinces. A consortium (composed of research institutions and companies spanning the whole milk chain, from dairy farms, feed producers, cattle reproduction, pharmaceutical production, dairy processors, consumers and industry organisations, the TGD, and competent authorities) run this project. Areas of this project include: reproduction, milk quality, and udder health and treatment (including strategies to reduce use of antibiotics); · OptiGene, funded by the association of Austrian Cattle Breeders. The objective of this project, completed in 2015, was to optimise the breeding of Austrian cattle breeds by 6 aligning it with the needs and demands of the farming systems in Austria, with special consideration to health and genomic selection; · Efficient Cow, funded by the Federal government and the provinces. The goal is to increase production efficiency in dairy cows by collecting data on milk production, body condition score and lameness, amongst others; · projects on hoof health (recently submitted) ­ to create an infrastructure on data-collection of animal care of hooves to identify which factors can help to avoid lameness ­ and for an electronic system to collect on-farm information on welfare indicators.

The Specialist Department for Animal Husbandry and Welfare (Fachstelle für tiergerechte Tierhaltung und Tierschutz) is an independent body financed by the Federal Ministry of Health on the basis of the Austrian Animal Welfare Act. Its task is to inspect husbandry and housing systems of farm and pet animals and novel products before placing them on the market. Products that pass the inspection by this Department bear an official welfare seal as a guarantee to clients that it will not affect the animals' health and welfare.

The regional authorities visited by the audit team identified EU Rural Development Funding as one of the actors helping to manage animal welfare on farms. Such funding is available for the restructuring of farms on the condition that they convert from tethering stalls to a loose- house system. In one of the provinces visited, 13% of the dairy farms (480 out of 3772) got funding under this scheme in the last five years. One of the farms visited by the audit team had converted recently from tethering to loose-house using these funds. According to the owner, this had led to a 40% increase in milk production and a significant improvement in milk quality (genetics remained the same). 5.2 ASSURANCES FROM COMPETENT AUTHORITY ACTIVITIES ON FARMERS' COMPLIANCE WITH LEGAL REQUIREMENTS Legal requirements Directive 98/58/EC. Commission Decision 2006/778/EC. Articles 3, 4, 6, 7, 17 and Appendix B of the Council of Europe Recommendation Concerning Cattle. Paragraphs 6 and 15 of Annex I to Directive 2008/119/EC. Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Findings

The country profile of Austria describes the structure of the authorities and the organisation of official controls in farms. It is accessible at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/country_profiles/details.cfm?co_id=AT. Additional information is available in the CCA's website at: http://bmgf.gv.at. 7

The CCA indicated that legislation applicable in the country on the protection of cattle in dairy farms, is in the Federal Law Gazette-FLG No 82/1993, as well as in the Austrian Federal Act on the Protection of Animals ­ Tierschutzgesetzes, which prohibits infliction of unnecessary pain, suffering or injury to an animal, or to put it under severe distress, and in the 1st Animal Husbandry Regulation ­ 1. Tierhaltungsverordnung.

The following official controls cover welfare of cattle at dairy farms: · regular inspections carried out for the purpose of cross-compliance (Regulation (EC) No 1698/20056). These include compliance checks against all the requirements of Directives 98/58/EC and 2008/119/EC amongst others. AgraMarkt Austria is provided with a copy of the inspection report; and · ad-hoc checks as a consequence of a complaint, suspicion or notification received from slaughterhouses, rendering plants or checks carried out by other bodies, such as the TGD. An official indicated that if the farm is a member of the TGD these controls are also used to audit the private veterinarian's annual farm evaluation (see also Paragraph 2).

The Animal Welfare Inspection Ordinance requires that at least 2% of all agricultural holdings are inspected annually (this are the regular inspections). The Agency for Health and Food Safety (Agentur für Gesundheit und Ernahrungssicherheit) selects the holdings at provincial level: · It chooses 80% of farms on the basis of identified risks- including those indicated by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004- and 20% of farms randomly; · the farms are selected from the list of holdings receiving single farm payments from AgraMarkt Austria. The provincial competent authorities indicated that the vast majority of dairy farms get single farm payments and only a very minimal percentage (less than 1%) do not get them.

The official veterinarians that check animal welfare at dairy farms have several tools (all readily available electronically) to prepare for the inspections, which they explained and demonstrated to the audit team. These include: · documented procedures, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in the form of handbooks which are publicly available. These include checklists and relevant guidelines that focus primarily on resource-based indicators but also include the use of animal-based indicators (e.g. body condition score and lameness) to evaluate some of these parameters. These documents are a comprehensive tool to perform animal welfare checks; · Databases kept by the competent authority and AgraMarkt Austria. With these, they can access information on the farm regarding past-controls, herd health status and number of animals; · information from the TGD database regarding farm production data (e.g. somatic cell count, milk quality, longevity, calving intervals, treatments, animals leaving the herd, including the reason) and the private veterinarian's farm evaluation reports. 6 Regulation (EC) No 1698/2005 (OJ L 277, 21.10.2005, p. 1­40) 8

The audit team visited two dairy farms, one farm keeping cattle in a tethered system with past non-compliances (that had already been corrected) due to high stocking density, and another that recently converted from a tethered system to loose-housing using EU Rural Development Funds. The official veterinarians demonstrated how inspections are performed. The controls were thorough and mainly resource-based. The official veterinarians also used animal-based indicators during their evaluation (body condition score for compliance with feeding requirements, hoof condition and presence of visible lesions for compliance with caring for animals and competent staff requirements). The officials performed the checks according to the procedures and documents.

The authorities use enforcement actions which include: reporting the non-compliance to AgraMarkt Austria (for cross-compliance purposes); written instruction to the farmer to correct the deficiencies- this instruction includes a deadline and it is followed up with a visit after this deadline- and, if a serious welfare infringement is detected, a report for legal proceedings. In the two Provinces visited, the audit team saw examples of enforcement actions in the inspection files reviewed.

A review of the reported animal welfare non-compliances for cattle (excluding calves) revealed that the most frequently ones detected in Austria in 2013 and 2014 was related to freedom of movement: · A deeper analysis from the detailed checklist indicated that this is generally linked to the requirement for access to pasture for a minimum of 90 days when cattle are kept on tethered farms. According to estimates7, 50-55% of dairy cattle farms use loose housing and 45-50% of the farms keep the cows tethered; · The authorities of the two provinces visited indicated that this type of non-compliance was not frequent in their territory due to the access to mountain pastures. The most frequent non-compliance in these two provinces was related to the small size of the stalls ­ they indicated this happens because the national regulation changed after these were built. The official controls in place provide assurances of compliance with animal welfare requirements for cattle in dairy farms. The various tools provided by both the authorities (documented procedures and own databases) and other actors involved (e.g. access to their databases) support the official veterinarians in keeping up to date with the farms' status and help them to better evaluate the welfare of cattle in dairy farms. 5.3 INDICATORS OF ANIMAL WELFARE Legal requirements Directive 98/58/EC. 7 Source: Federal Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water Management. 9 Articles 3, 4, 6, 7, 17 and Appendix B of the Council of Europe Recommendation Concerning Cattle. recommendations.text: Ensure that sampling methodology applied for plant health checks is based on the risk of the presence of harmful organisms, such as to conclude from these checks that the lot is not contaminated by harmful organisms, in line with Article 13(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The recommendation is based on conclusion No.29. Associated findings No.17, 18, 20 and 22.

citations.text: All plants intended for planting (other than aquatic plants), including seed, are categorised as high-risk. Low-risk plants include all aquatic plants; and fruits, vegetables and cut flowers imported between October and April. All other plants and plant products fall into the medium-risk category.

The BAES explained that aquatic plants are categorised as low-risk due to the intended use of these plants (presumed to be placed into aquaria), which means the likelihood of any harmful organisms which may be present transferring to other host plants is low. The BAES also explained that seasonality is a key criterion in determining the risk of fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, because of the cold climatic conditions in Austria between October and April, which means that any harmful organisms present would not be able to establish in their territory. The BAES went on to explain that these types of products were, to the best of their knowledge, always destined for customers in Austria.

During a visit to Vienna airport, the audit team observed an inspection being carried out of a consignment from Thailand containing mixed plant produce, including three regulated articles, aubergines (Solanum melongena); mangoes (Mangifera indica); and 6 orchid cut flowers (Dendrobium sp.). All three regulated lots were categorised as 'low- risk' for the purpose of determining the size of sample to take for visual checks. However, at the time of the audit, orchid cut flowers featured on the non-EU trade Alert List3 due to repeated interceptions notified by EU Member States. The BAES inspectors stated that based on their own experiences of regular consignments of the same exporter and the same produce, where no interception was recorded in the past, they considered the pre-export treatments to be reliable and the risk of finding live pest to be low, and restated the low likelihood of any live pest being able to establish in Austria at that time of year.

The sampling methodology applied for plant health checks of aquatic plants, fruits, vegetables and cut flowers is determined according to the risk posed to the Austrian territory by any harmful organism which may be present, rather than the risk of the lot being contaminated by harmful organisms. This is not line with Article 13(1)(i) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The sampling methodology applied for plant health checks of aquatic plants, fruits, vegetables and cut flowers, is not based on the risk of the presence of harmful organisms. It is not therefore ensured that it can be concluded, as a result of these checks, that the lot is not contaminated with harmful organisms. 5.2 COOPERATION AND COMMUNICATION WITH CUSTOMS SERVICES AND STAKEHOLDERS Legal requirements Articles 2(1) and 13(1) of Council Directive 2000/29/EC Article 6 of Commission Directive 2004/103/EC. audits.title: Feed additives, their ingredients and traceability

recommendations.text: To ensure that feed business operators ' establishments are appropriately approved and that the approval status is under regular review of approval status as required by Article 31(2(e)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 9. Associated findings: 5, 6 and 7.

citations.text: Shortcomings were noted on the approval status and processes at the establishments visited by the audit team. In some cases FeBOs had been wrongly categorised as approved feed additive producers when in fact they were intermediate food and feed material producers, and for which only registration was necessary, and there were registered FeBOs producing certain feed additives for which approval was necessary (but had not been given). These shortcomings had recently been noted by the competent authority during the preparation of this audit and both issues are linked to the fact that the approval of FeBOs is not regularly reviewed during official inspections. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 31(2(f)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

As regards to the implementation of the approval procedure, examples were seen where all the steps were appropriately followed including comprehensive onsite approval inspections. Nevertheless, shortcomings and/or inconsistencies were noted in some of the establishments visited. These ranged from a lack of inspection visits and/or reports for approvals for which such inspection was required, to an incomplete list of relevant documentation which would have demonstrated that all of the approval steps had been performed. The lack of inspection visits not in line with the requirements laid down by 3 Article 31(2(e)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 13(1) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

The audit team was also informed that a full re-approval process was triggered with the entry into force of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Nevertheless, this had not been consistently applied at the FeBOs visited, with some steps of the official approval process either being by-passed (e.g., neither a technical assessment nor onsite inspection being carried out) or added beyond agreed procedures with no plausible explanation given (e.g. onsite inspection of traders). Conclusion on the structure of the system for official controls on feed additives and ingredients for their production

Whilst there is a clear registration and approval procedure for FeBOs' in place, inconsistencies in the implementation of the approval procedure, together with lack of regular review during official controls, resulted in deficiencies on the approval of FeBOs. 5.2 PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL FEED CONTROLS 5.2.1 Inspections 5.2.1.1 PLANNING OF INSPECTIONS

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls, which are planned following a risk-based system, are implemented in accordance with the system, as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 12 Recommendation based on conclusion: 28. Associated findings: 14, and 15.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the number of planned routine controls had not been reached for at least the previous three years. As explained by the competent authority, this was due to human resource constraints, structural changes, the processing of available data, and outstanding inspection cases from previous years. Consequently the stated risk- based frequency of inspections is not being met. Furthermore, official controls that are performed at feed establishments no longer follow the planned risk-based criteria.

In the case of comprehensive inspections, the frequency is set once every three years but solely applying to the higher two categories of producing FeBOs and all feed additive producers, and only the higher category of non-producing FeBOs. As with routine controls, examples were seen of comprehensive inspection frequencies not being met. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The competent authorities have a risk-based control plan in place covering feed additives, their ingredients and traceability, but their failure to consistently adhere to 7 planned arrangements and select establishments for inspections on the basis of established risk criteria weakens the efficiency of the control system.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls check that feed business operators meet the requirements, related to retained samples, laid down by the section "QUALITY CONTROL"(4) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. Recommendation based on conclusion: 29. Associated findings: 24.

citations.text: FeBOs' retained samples are labelled to enable appropriate traceability and stored for at least as long as the given shelf-life of the product. However, only a minority of FeBOs visited had retained samples which were appropriately sealed to avoid the possibility of tampering. In addition, in the majority of FeBOs visited there were no adequate written procedures to take such samples. The BAES inspections covered the issue of retained samples, however, in none of the establishments visited had the absence of appropriate sealing been identified as requiring corrective action. This is not in line with the section "QUALITY CONTROL"(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 5.2.1.2.2 Labelling

The appropriate level of competency and knowledge were shown by all relevant competent authorities. Official controls targeted the relevant areas of feed business operators' obligations such as the implementations of HACCP based procedures, own control programmes including traceability, labelling and sampling. However, official controls did not verify that feed business operators met their obligation as regards the retention of samples. This weakens the effectives of the system of official feed controls. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

recommendations.text: To ensure that final samples are prepared in accordance with the requirements laid down by part 9.4 of Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Recommendation based on conclusion: 39. Associated findings: 35 and 36.

citations.text: The audit team presented the BAES inspectors with various sampling scenarios and in all instances, they were able to quickly analyse the situation, and upon consulting the legislation, present the correct sampling procedural plan. Nevertheless, a systemic shortcoming was noted, in that the preparation of final samples from the aggregate sample was performed by simple manual mixing. This practice cannot ensure the appropriate homogenisation as required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

The sampling equipment observed, whilst appropriate for sampling in certain conditions, did not allow sampling throughout the sampled portion when the product is stored in large bags or in bulk form. This is not in line with the requirements laid down by part 4 and 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

Planning of official sampling is risk-based and the implementation, for the most part, is adequate, being carried out by staff with the requisite competence and expertise. Notwithstanding this, inadequate homogenisation of sampled materials and the absence of a suitable sampling tool for large volumes collectively undermine the effectiveness of the sampling programme and the legal and analytical validity of some of the official samples taken. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that when the competent authority identifies non-compliance, it takes action to ensure that the operator remedies the situation as required by Article 54(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Recommendation based on conclusion: 45. Associated findings: 42, 43 and 44.

citations.text: The audit team saw several examples of such warning letters for minor and major non- compliances. The FeBOs visited were able to demonstrate that, following their internal analyses and investigations, corrective actions had been taken.

With regard to the BAES' monitoring, follow-up and escalation of enforcement of unaddressed non-compliances, the audit team observed that in the case of the three major non-compliances presented as examples, in two of these, four weeks were given to the FeBOs to take appropriate action, with the follow up inspection only taking place around one and a half years after the original inspection visit. In the third case from the latter months of 2016, no date for corrective action had been given nor had follow-up yet taken place. Furthermore, after a negative inspection result on the first two cases, the BAES had informed the district level on the need to impose a fine on the FeBOs, but no information was available to indicate that this had actually been done, or whether the non-compliances had been finally appropriately addressed by the FeBOs.

In the case of minor non-compliances, for which a time-scale for corrective action is, as defined in the BAES procedures, not given to FeBOs, there is no reporting mechanism, either by the FeBOs or the BAES inspectors, on corrective actions (if any) being taken. Thus it is not ensured that the FeBOs have addressed minor non-compliances, which is not in line with Article 54(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusion on actions taken on non-compliances

Whilst there is a well-structured system for the identification and categorisation of non- compliances and initial communication to FeBOs requesting corrective action, its effectiveness is undermined by either an absence of monitoring or a much delayed follow-up of such non-compliances. BAES is unaware as to the level of resolution of non-compliances and is unaware of those unresolved non-compliances which would warrant an escalation of official enforcement. 10 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives but are exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a third country

recommendations.text: To ensure that documentary checks for consignments of products of animal origin provided for in Article 4(3) of Directive 97/78/EC are carried out in line with Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and for consignments of live animals in accordance with the rules laid down in Annex I to Decision 97/794/EC in order that only eligible consignments are imported into the EU. Recommendation based on conclusion: 69 Associated findings: 41, 48, 49 and 57

citations.text: The controls on live animals were, based on the documentation checked by the audit team, in general well-implemented with a few exceptions: the Combined Nomenclature - CN code mentioned in part I of some common veterinary entry documents for animals (CVEDAs) did not cover all fish species, crustaceans, molluscs or corals; the catch area of wild fish was not mentioned on some other health certificates examined by the audit team. These omissions had not been noticed by the BIP staff. The audit team noted that in 2017 some registered equidae had entered Austria from Serbia as temporary admissions. Some of the animals had been converted into permanent imports contrary to the declaration in part IV of the health certificate in Annex II.B to Commission Decision 92/260/EEC and the instructions in the BIP manual. According to the requirements for import of registered equidae in the health certificate in Annex II.B to Commission Decision 93/197/EEC, the equidae have to be quarantined in the country of origin for 90 days, whereas in this case the equidae were subject to less stringent import conditions (quarantined in Austria for one month only and tested for malleus, 7 equine infectious anaemia and Trypanosoma equiperdum) before being released for free circulation. 5.2.3.2 Checks on products of animal origin including sampling

The audit team noticed the following shortcomings related to the documentary checks of products of animal origin: a) A consignment of raw hides from a non-approved establishment was allowed for further processing. This is not in line with point 2(f) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. b) One consignment of casings was imported, but the accompanying health certificate differed from the model health certificate. This is not in line with point 2(c) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 136/2004. 8 c) A consignment of a blood preparation was exported from Austria to a third country without an export certificate. The consignment was re-imported without the original export certificate containing details of the reasons for refusal and a non-manipulation declaration. This is not in line with Article 15 of Directive 97/78/EC. National provisions were applied to allow the re-importation of this consignment. d) Instructions for checking the authenticity of Chinese certificates were available at the BIPs but the BIPs did not have the correct equipment to check all the safety features (no fluorescent lamps were available and no magnifying glass with the required 20x magnification).

A number of CVEDPs examined by the audit team had been accepted even though there were discrepancies in the content of the health certificate e.g. chilled instead of frozen meat, carcasses versus packed meat. These had not been noted by the BIP staff during their controls. 5.2.3.3 Implementation of controls on food and feed of non-animal origin

There is a system in place for channelling of products according to Article 8 of Directive 97/78/EC. Evidence was available that in addition to the use of TRACES the pre-notified consignments are registered in a logbook. Confirmation of arrival at the establishments of destination is received via e-mail and thereafter registered in 9 TRACES by BIP staff. The audit team identified some shortcomings regarding the channelling of products, in particular related to the awareness of the approval of the physical place of destination within Austria or in another Member State.

The implementation of the import controls on live animals and feed and food of both animal and non-animal origin was generally in line with EU legislation, though there were shortcomings in the implementation of documentary checks on some consignments of live animals and products of animal origin, weakening assurances that only compliant consignments are imported into the EU via the BIPs in question.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the facilities in BIP/DPE Linz for products comply with the relevant requirements laid down in Article 4.1 of and the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC (products of animal origin) and Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 669/2009 (products of non-animal origi based on conclusion: 82 Associated findings: 78 and 81

citations.text: The facilities for products were adequate except for the loading area, where the ceiling was leaking. The competent authority stated that it was in touch with the airport authority to address this issue.
The audit team identified rodent activity at the BIP, which had not been identified by the BIP staff. Conclusions on the suitability of facilities

The facilities, equipment and hygiene of both BIP/DPEs were in general adequate for undertaking import controls though maintenance works were required in the BIP/DPE Linz. 6. OVERALL CONCLUSIONS The audit found that the framework for official controls on imports of animals, food and feed facilitated efficient coordination and cooperation within and between the various competent authorities involved. Personnel were qualified and trained to undertake their duties competently and to carry out official controls in a consistent manner in the framework of a system supported by documented procedures and well developed computer-based information technology. In that regard, the use of the Trade Control and Expert System - TRACES - for products of non- animal origin, which goes beyond what is required by EU legislation, contributes to the EU- wide traceability of such goods. Whilst the implementation of controls on imports of live animals and feed and food of both animal and non-animal origin was generally in line with EU legislation, shortcomings in the implementation of documentary checks on some consignments of live animals and products of animal origin weaken assurances that only compliant consignments are imported into the EU via the BIPs in question. These shortcomings were not detected by the supervisory 12 system in place. As regards facilities and equipment, these were in general satisfactory in the country's two border inspection posts/designated points of entry, though improved maintenance and pest control is clearly needed in one of the facilities visited by the audit team. 7. At this meeting, the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit were presented by the audit team. The central competent authority did not express disagreement with the findings and conclusions presented and provided some additional clarifications. 8. RECOMMENDATIONS No. Recommendation 1. recommendations.text: Ensure that the designated competent authorities implement and enforce controls at all stages of primary production, in line with Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and with a view to covering microbiological risks along the entire production chai based on conclusion 6, 16, and 59. Associated findings: 3, 4, 5, 38, 39 and 40.

citations.text: The main national legislation in the context of this audit is the Food Safety and Consumer Protection Act (LMSVG), Federal Law Gazette of the Republic of Austria (BGBI) I No. 13/2006.3 This act covers the EU food law and Hygiene Package. The scope of the Law is described in paragraph 1(1) and comprises the requirements for food, water for human consumption, utensils and cosmetic products and the associated responsibility of the FBO. It applies to all stages of production, processing and distribution. It does not apply to primary production for private domestic use or to the domestic processing, handling or storage of food, commodities and cosmetic products for domestic private consumption. Paragraph 11 obliges BMASGK to provide by ordinance hygiene regulations for the direct delivery of small quantities of, inter alia, primary products by the producer to the final consumer or to local retailers which deliver the products directly to the final consumer. The Ordinance BGBI II No. 108/2006 covers this obligation. Paragraph 15 empowers the BMASGK to adopt more detailed regulations by way of implementing the provisions of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, after consultation with the BMNT. Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 lays down the general hygiene provisions for primary production and contains recommendations for guides to good hygiene practice. They are directly applicable in the MS. There are no implementing provisions drafted by BMAGSK to cover these provisions. 3 All legislation is made available to the public on the BGBI website: http://www.ris.bka.gv.at/ 4 Paragraph 24 designates the Governors of the Provinces as CA for the official controls in the scope of this audit and in particular to implement the official controls regarding the provisions for official controls on microbiological risks before and during harvest.

Several BMASGK guidelines are in place, in particular regarding: health requirements for persons handling food after harvest; staff training handling food after harvest; fruit processing at farms after harvest.
The Chamber of Agriculture of Austria has published guidelines on hygiene and own controls for direct suppliers after harvest. Conclusions on relevant national legislation and guidelines

The legal provisions in place designate and empower CAs at central and provincial level for the implementation of official controls on microbiological risks in the whole production chain, including primary production. 5.2 ORGANISATION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF OFFICIAL CONTROLS 5.2.1 Designation of competent authorities and resources for official controls Legal requirements Article 4(1) Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 Designation of competent authorities

There are central and regional CAs designated by national legislation regarding official controls on microbiological risks at all stages of production. However, the central and regional CAs did not act to implement such controls before and during harvest, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Therefore, a considerable part of the FNAO production is not covered by the official control system.

The audit team visited five growers in two different Provinces. All growers had packing facilities and were direct sellers or distributing to retailers. In all visited premises, inspectors stated that they only carry out inspections if the primary production is linked to direct sales or the distribution to retail chains.

The inspections took place at the facilities where produce was received, cleaned, packed and stored. The inspectors followed the four modules of the checklist "producer" which cover facilities and equipment, produce and handling, hygiene and training and documentary checks.

citations.text: Methods are validated according to an in-house validation procedure, which is based on requirements laid down in Decision 2002/657/EC. The samples are required to be spiked at three concentration levels with six repetitions as required in point 3.1.2.2 of the aforementioned decision, thus recommendation No 4 of the 2011 audit report has been addressed. However, one parameter, the within-laboratory reproducibility, is not part of the formalised validation plan, which is not in line with the requirements laid down in point 3.1.2.3 of the Annex I to Commission decision 2002/657/EC. Nonetheless, the competent authority can have confidence in the reliability of the result given the other quality assurance measures in place as outlined below. This was verified by the audit team on-the-spot when assessing the validation of the confirmatory methods for gestagens (A3) and macrolides (B1).

For all confirmatory methods, as ongoing quality assurance, two calibration curves are included in each analytical series (one at the beginning, one at the end). Furthermore quality control samples, blank samples and fortified samples are run with each sequence and internal standards are used regularly as far as possible. This is in line with the requirements of point 2.3.1 of Annex 1 to Decision 2002/657/EC. The recovery from the fortified samples is used for a recovery correction. Newly prepared standard solutions are checked against old standard solutions. The spiking solution for recovery control samples are different from those used for the preparation of the calibration curves. Quality control charts were not systematically used for all methods, but only for frequently used ones. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in Article 5 of Decision 2002/657/EC and in point 5.9 of ISO 17025:2005 as it does not allow the detection of trends in the method performance. 7

At the wholesaler and the veterinary practitioner of the para-pharmacy visited by the audit team, an electronic system was in use, which fulfilled the record-keeping requirements and the annually required comparison between incoming and outgoing medicinal supplies, as foreseen in Article 65(3) of Directive 2001/82/EC.

citations.text: In the provinces of Upper and Lower Austria, the audit team visited four establishments approved before the application of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. The original approval certificates including information on original activities were not available. Nonetheless, new approval numbers had been assigned automatically under national legislation, Article 10(2) of the LMSVG. The audit team noted that there is no documented guidance regarding the issuing of new approval numbers to these establishments. The approval letters issued by the CA did not specify what processing activities the FBOs were approved for nor the conditions of approval­ such as the obligation to inform the CA of changes in the circumstances of approval as required under national law, BGB1.II No 231/2009. Thus jeopardising compliance with national legislation and Article 6 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 that requires FBOs to ensure that the CA has always up-dated information on establishments, including by notifying any significant change in activities and any closure of an existing establishment. According to the national legislation, the need to notify the provincial CA includes a "substantial change in production conditions". The audit team noted that for one of the officials interviewed, this statement meant changing the type of production from fish to meat but not starting the production of, for example, smoked fish.

In Vienna, an establishment visited had been approved before the application of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, but the CA had also issued a new approval certificate, specifying that it was also approved for a new activity of processing smoked products.

However, in four out of five re-approved establishments, the approval letter did not specify what processing activities they were approved for nor the need to notify the authorities if there was any change in production conditions as required under national law. citations.text: The inspections scrutinised by the Commission auditor covered registration/approval, pre-requisites of HACCP (e.g. cleaning, pest control), identification of ingredients, intermediate and final products (relating to traceability) and general hygiene of facilities and equipment. These inspections also checked the availability of documentation relating to the FeBO`s HACCP-plan and own control system (e.g., hazard analyses, critical control points, corrective measures, monitoring plans and results for undesirable substances and/or microbiological contaminants, homogeneity and cross-contamination tests) but not their adequacy since BAES inspectors do not carry out a comprehensive assessment of these documents. Instead, they forward part or all of the documentation to the AGES for further assessment. AGES' experts assess the documents (not necessarily all of them) and report to the BAES any non-compliances identified. Such arrangements considerably complicate the verification by the competent authorities that FeBOs implement the requirements laid down in Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

Where relevant, the Commission auditor scrutinised the assessment by the feed inspectors of hazard analyses, and tests on efficiency of mixing (homogeneity) and cross-contamination with coccidiostats. The auditor noted that in three of the nine FeBOs scrutinised, the hazard analyses were incomplete (they were either very general and/or several potential hazards were missing or not assessed) even if these operators were regularly controlled during the previous years (see finding 18). At one operator where the cross-contamination test was discussed, the BAES inspectors interviewed experienced difficulties to adequately carry out the assessment of the relevant documents. In principle, these assessments are carried out by the AGES, not by the BAES officials on-the-spot. The AGES officials stated that they had have never assessed the requested documents before, however they did demonstrate good knowledge of the assessment criteria.

In the documentation of the cross-contamination tests seen, the method of sampling, which is an essential element of related assessment, was not described, which complicates the assessment of the said testing. While the AGES officials interviewed did identify this as a non-compliance during the interview with the Commission auditor, the BAES inspection report seen did not contain the corresponding finding. The assessment of cross-contamination tests is not part of the BAES inspections.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and ensures that the official inspections are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. Notwithstanding that the inspections largely adequately address 7 pertinent legal requirements on feed hygiene, the lack of a comprehensive assessment of the appropriateness of the FeBOs' HACCP plans and own-check programmes weakens the effectiveness of the system. 5.2.2 SAMPLING 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

citations.text: Authorisation is carried out together with the registration. However, operators authorised to issue plant passports before 2019 had to request their re-authorisation to meet the amended EU requirements. During the initial official control, inspectors check 5 whether the operator complies with the criteria of authorisation, however, it is not verified whether the operator possesses the necessary knowledge to carry out examinations as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 17). The decision on authorisation contains the types of plants for which the operator is authorised to issue plant passports and a detailed description of their obligations. The authorisation is valid indefinitely.

The audit team observed that, contrary to Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, during the official control the inspectors did not verify the compliance with the following requirements (see also section 5.4.1): a. whether authorised operators carry out meticulous examination to show that their plants, plant products and other objects fulfil the EU requirements, and whether the results of these examinations have been recorded and stored for at least three years, as required by Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, b. whether authorised operators possess the necessary knowledge to carry out such examinations as required by Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, c. whether authorised operators identify and monitor the points of their production process and the points concerning the movement of plants, plant products and 6 other objects, which are critical as regards compliance with the EU requirements and if they keep records concerning the identification and monitoring of those points for at least three years, as required by Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, d. whether authorised operators provide appropriate training, when necessary, to their personnel involved in the examinations, as required by Article 90(2) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on authorisation and supervision of professional operators for issuing plant passports

The compliance of professional operators who applied to issue plant passport with EU requirements is not appropriately verified during the authorisation procedure and the annual official controls. Therefore, there is a risk that plant passports are issued by professional operators who do not possess the necessary knowledge to carry out examinations, consequently increasing the phytosanitary risks of plants moved within the EU. 5.4 EXAMINATIONS FOR THE ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 85 to 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Findings 5.4.1 Examinations by authorised operators

The audit team visited five professional operators authorised to issue plant passports and observed the following (see also finding 17): a. The operators had a good knowledge about the plants they produce and about the common, non-regulated pests against which they apply treatments. Each of them attended the mandatory training (see finding 14), however they did not know the most important regulated pests that could affect their plants and the symptoms caused by them. Consequently, they did not possess the necessary knowledge to carry out the examinations required by EU law contrary to Article 89(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. b. The operators regularly carried out examinations regarding the health status of their plants in order to plan treatments against common, non-regulated pests. These examinations did not show that the plants fulfil the EU requirements 7 regarding regulated pests, relevant results have not been recorded, contrary to Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. c. Each authorised operator confirmed that they did not identify and monitor the points of their production process and the points concerning the movement of plants, plant products and other objects, which are critical as regards compliance with the EU requirements and did not keep such records, contrary to Article 90(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. d. Each authorised operator confirmed that they did not provide training to their personnel involved in the examinations to ensure that they possess the necessary knowledge to carry out such examinations. 5.4.2 Examinations by competent authorities including the verification of examinations carried out by authorised operators

The inspectors met were aware of the EU requirements, the regulated pests and demonstrated meticulous examinations. The audit team noted that these inspections were done in line with the documented procedures at appropriate times with regard to the possibility of detecting the presence of pests, their signs or symptoms. However, verification of the examinations carried out by authorised operators was not done by the inspectors, contrary to Article 92(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 5.4.3 Examinations in relation to the protected zones

Authorised operators met by the audit team do not carry out meticulous examinations to verify that their plants fulfil the EU requirements, therefore their examinations do not provide sufficient guarantee for the issuance of plant passports.

The CAs do not verify whether authorised operators carry out the required examinations. The authorised operators met by the audit team did not possess the necessary knowledge to carry out such examinations. This demonstrates the need for further awareness raising and training of authorised operators on the plant passport requirements. 5.5 ISSUANCE OF PLANT PASSPORTS, INCLUDING RECORD KEEPING Legal requirements Articles 69, 70 and 87 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 in its entirety Regulation (EU) 2019/827 in its entirety Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.5.1 Issuance of plant passports by competent authorities

In Austria, all plant passports are issued by authorised operators under the supervision of the CAs, including those combined with certification labels, however, this is not always based on a meticulous examination as required by Article 87 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 (see also finding 20). In line with EU requirements, the application of trade unit is not limited, it can be one plant or even a whole consignment with any combination of species and origins, provided that the traceability is guaranteed. The traceability code can be any kind of code used by the authorised operator to identify each trade unit. The audit team noted, that contrary to the Annex of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2017/2313 ­ which provides that the required flag of the Union may be printed in colour (yellow stars on blue background), or in black and white, either with white stars on a black background, or vice versa ­ a different colour of the substrate is also accepted as a background to the EU flag.

Meticulous examinations are not always carried out to verify compliance with EU requirements, therefore the issued plant passports do not provide sufficient guarantee that the plants fulfil the EU requirements, which increases the phytosanitary risk of plants moved within the EU. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS ON MOVEMENT OF PLANTS AND PLANT PRODUCTS WITH PLANT PASSPORTS Legal requirements Articles 69, 79 to 83, 88 and 93 to 95 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 Articles 2 to 6, 8(2), 9, 10, 13, 14 and 17 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 Articles 1 to 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/66 Regulation (EU) 2020/1770 in its entirety Findings 5.6.1 Official controls on traceability

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on ABP plants, establishments and operators are carried out without prior notification, except when duly justified. Legal basis: Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: 62 Associated finding: 31
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: 62 Associated finding: 31

citations.text: All district veterinary inspectors met confirmed that inspections of ABP plants are carried out with prior notification and that unannounced inspections are the exception. In some cases, inspections are announced one or two days before the due date and, in other cases, up to a week in advance, when the inspectors prepare their weekly schedule of activities. Routine prior notification of inspections in not in line with Article 9(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Official controls at ABP plants are largely effective to verify infrastructural and hygiene requirements. However, they are usually notified in advance and they do not pay sufficient attention to the implementation of HACCP-based procedures and the operators' own checks. Similarly, checks on the validation of processing plants remain limited or poorly documented. All of this limits the ability of the competent authorities to verify whether ABP and DP are handled and processed to the high safety standards provided for in EU legislation.

citations.text: The food inspectors met stated that they had not received training on ABP and that in the absence of knowledge of the rules applicable to ABP, they were not able to critically assess the degree of compliance of the food operators in this area. They stated that their main point of attention was to verify that food and waste (this included ABP for the food inspectors) were adequately separated and that there was no contamination of food by waste.

The audit team reviewed several records of inspections carried out by food inspectors at randomly chosen food operators. From these records, it was visible that some information was available on the type of ABP produced by the operators and the operators collecting them. However, the food inspectors met stated that such information was collected but not assessed. For instance, they did not check the presence of commercial documentation or if the operator collecting such ABP was approved for handling these types of ABP.

The audit team reviewed some cases where non-conformities were identified in relation to ABP at some operators under the supervision of food inspectors. These cases were either identified by the inspectors or were investigated following complaints. From the discussion held with the audit team, it was clear that in the few cases where food inspectors had some knowledge of ABP or had investigated ABP-related complaints, they were able to adequately follow-up on such issues, in particular by liaising with the veterinary inspectors in charge of controls at ABP operators.

The food inspectors met stated that, at retailers, they verified that meat and meat products not fit for human consumption (e.g., products with expired shelf life or spoiled meat) were kept separated from food. They also verified that unsold food of animal origin was not given to farmers for feeding their animals. They confirmed that no other checks were carried out to ascertain the destination of ABP as this was, in their opinion, the responsibility of the business operator to dispose of them in line with the applicable rules.

Based on the above findings, the audit team noted that official controls carried by food inspectors at food business operators are not suitable to verify compliance with ABP rules, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(3) of Regulation No 1069/2009.

In contrast, for food business operators under supervision of the food inspectorates (e.g. milk, eggs, fish and retail sectors) official controls are inadequate, mainly due to 13 insufficient knowledge of ABP requirements, to monitor the correct handling, use and disposal of such materials. This weakens the guarantees that ABP and DP generated by food business operators are collected and disposed of in line with EU rules.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the national legislation concerning the direct supply by the producer of small quantities of milk and milk products produced on a holding is in line with Articles 1(4) and 1(5)(b) of Regulation (EC) 853/2004 to achieve the objectives of the Regulation with regard to the local placing on the market of small quantities of milk and dairy products directly by the food business operator producing them. Recommendation based on conclusion No 4. Associated finding No 1(d.)

citations.text: The main national legislation covering the safety of milk and dairy products comprises: a. The Food Safety and Consumer Protection Act (Lebensmittesicherheits- und Verbraucherschutzgesetz), as amended, provides the CAs with powers to carry out inspections and audits, and to initiate enforcement measures. b. The Raw milk Ordinance (Rohmilchverordnung) regulates the direct sale of raw milk and cream by the keeper of the animals for immediate human consumption by the final consumer or to retail for immediate sale to the final consumer. It prohibits the sale of raw milk/cream to schools and creches. Other types of catering companies can only use it after effective heat treatment. Raw milk can also be delivered via milk automates on the day of production and the following two days provided its safety not impacted. Consumers must be informed that the milk can only be consumed after boiling and that the cream can only be used for dishes that are thoroughly heated. If the product is sold to retail the information must be available on the delivery note. The raw milk has to comply with strict criteria for PC and SCC. c. The Food Hygiene Direct Marketing Ordinance, (Lebensmittelhygiene- Direktvermarktungsverordnung) contains the national rules for milk and dairy products related to Article 1(2)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 and Article 3 1(3)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 (direct supply of small quantities of primary products to the final consumer or to local retail establishments directly supplying the final consumer). d. The Food Hygiene Direct Marketing Ordinance (Lebensmittelhygiene- Einzelhandelsverordnung) regulates the specific hygiene requirements for food of animal origin for retail, which do not fall under the rules of Article 1.5 (a) or (b) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. It allows the dairy holding to sell raw milk and fermented milk products to retail if these are then sold directly to the final consumer or treated further only based on the consumer's request or used for products that do not fall under Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Although this activity is classified as a "marginal, localised and restricted activity" cf. Article 1 paragraph 5, point b)ii of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, such products can be sold in the whole country. Austria has not adopted derogations for traditional methods or for food business operator (FBO) situated in regions with geographical constraints (Art 10(3)-(8) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

The interpretation and implementation of "marginal, localised and restricted activity" in the Food Hygiene Direct Marketing Ordinance is not in line with the provisions of Article 1, paragraph 5, point b(ii) of Regulation (EC) N 853/2004. 5.2 COMPETENT AUTHORITIES Legal requirements Articles 4 and 5 of, and Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that effective coordination and cooperation is in place between the veterinary and food safety units at Land level as laid down in Article 5.5 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to ensure the food safety unit is informed of findings on dairy holdings that are relevant for food safety. Recommendation based on conclusion No 15. Associated finding Nos 9, 37 and 59.

citations.text: The information flow between the veterinary and food authorities in case of suspicion of bovine tuberculosis and in relation to detection of residues of veterinary medicinal products at Land level demonstrated some gaps (see paragraphs 37 and 59).
The exchange of information between the veterinary service and public health service at Land level has some gaps that reduce the effectivity of the controls (see paragraphs 37 and 59).

The audit team checked a file regarding a bovine milk production holding which was suspected to have animals infected with M. caprae. The actions taken were in line with the legal requirements of the Bovine Tuberculosis Ordinance (Rinder- Tuberkuloseverordnung). Evidence was available that milk from the holding, derived from suspect animals, was sent either to a composting or a biogas plant as category 2 animal by-product (ABP). The information flow between the veterinary and food control authorities in case of suspicion revealed some gaps. The dairy that had received the milk before the suspicion had refused to receive the milk from clinically healthy animals after the suspicion was known. The food inspector in charge of the establishment had not been informed what happened with the milk from the healthy animals thereafter and stated he would only be informed when the ban was lifted. The official veterinarian responsible 8 for the controls on the holding stated to have checked this aspect, but that this was not documented.

In Styria and Tyrol, information regarding residues of VMPs detected in raw milk is provided only to the veterinary services. The food inspector from Styria interviewed stated they had requested to also receive this information, as they are responsible for the control of direct sales from the holdings.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the approval procedure of dairy establishments is in line with the provisions of Article 148 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 regarding conditional approval (that can be granted for 3 months and prolonged once for an additional 3 months only after a second official control), and that approvals are kept under review. Recommendation based on conclusions Nos 30 and 31. Associated findings Nos 23, 24 and 25.

citations.text: Contrary to the requirements of Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 the national legislation permits the issuing of a temporary approval up to 6 months in one step, and the audit team noted this possibility had been used in one establishment file examined.

The approvals issued by the Länder vary in format. Some (e.g. Styria and Upper Austria) include the products range in the approval, some don't (e.g. Tyrol), and some do it for more recent approvals. In Tyrol some long existing FBOs had approvals that were dated back to the 1990s and where the legal basis was old, revoked legislation. The food inspectors interviewed stated that they would know the product range by going through the files of the establishments in the databases. However, the general checklist for dairy inspections did not include a verification of the approval against the activities on the spot. The inspector in one Land stated to use his own checklist for his purpose.

The audit team found a deep freezer in one dairy establishment, used by farmers to deposit colostrum for a dairy FBO located in another Member State. The deep freezer was owned by the foreign dairy and the CA responsible for the controls of the establishment visited was unaware of this activity, which was not subject to an official or own control. Another establishment produced a non-dairy product, which was not included in the approval; the responsible CA was not aware of this activity.
The Approval Ordinance is not fully in line with the equivalent EU legislation.

The CAs do not keep the approvals under review in a fully effective manner, and consequently are not aware of all changes in FBOs' activities. 5.4 CONTROLS OVER MILK AND COLOSTRUM PRODUCTION HOLDINGS Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I of Section IX, Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 49 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that controls of dairy holdings as laid down in Article 49 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 cover all relevant species, that the inspections are carried out as planned and that mechanisms are in place to provide the central competent authority an overview of the situatio based on conclusion No 45. Associated findings Nos 40 and 42.

citations.text: No harmonised programme is in place for verification of hygiene of primary milk production. The organisation of controls on the hygiene on milk and colostrum on dairy holdings is left to the Länder and the CCA had no overview of the situation, especially regarding goat and sheep dairy production holdings. The Länder Upper and Lower Austria, Styria, and Burgenland use AGES to select the holdings to be visited based on certain risk criteria, the other Länder choose the holdings to be inspected themselves. The controls are usually combined with other controls, e.g. cross-compliance controls, controls on animal welfare, on the use of veterinary medicinal products (VMPs) or animal health controls. Some Länder are using a targeted checklist (e.g. Tyrol), and other have included some questions in other checklists but the single checklists do not always cover all specific points as laid down in Chapters I and II of Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

The national statistics on inspections of dairy goat and sheep holdings did not match the data from the Länder (for example, in 2021 the number of inspections planned and carried out on goat and sheep dairy holdings was 42 in the national statistics, whereas the number of inspections in Upper Austria was 69 planned and 25 carried out and in Styria there were 10 planned and 5 carried out). Although no inspections of dairy sheep and goat holdings were planned for 2019,2020 and 2021 in Tyrol, the number of annual inspections carried out was 4, 15 and 5, respectively. The CA of Upper Austria stated that no training has been organised on this topic (2). (2) In their response to the draft report, the competent authority noted that a training course for officials on how to carry out milking hygiene inspections on farms was planned for the next in-service meeting (5 and 6 October 2023). 9

The verification of compliance with hygiene regulatory requirements is carried out on a limited percentage of holdings and the CCA has no overview of the situation, especially in relation to goat and sheep milk production holdings. 5.5 CONTROLS ON RAW MILK UPON COLLECTION Legal requirements Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Article 3 of, and Chapter I, Part III, Section IX of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. Article 50 of, and Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Findings

Associated findings Nos 55, 56 and 57. To ensure that official controls, and where necessary enforcement of food business operators' compliance regarding procedures based on HACCP principles, as laid down in Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004 and 853/2004 and 2073/2005, are effective as required by Article 18.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and cover all relevant requireme based on conclusion No 86. Associated findings Nos 77 and 82. To ensure that official controls, and where necessary enforcement of food business operators' compliance with labelling and traceability rules for dairy products, as laid down in Regulations (EC) Nos 852/2004, 853/2004 and Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, are effective as required by Article 18.1 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion No 86. Associated findings Nos 83 and 84.

citations.text: The method used in the AMA-listed laboratories for detection of residues of VMPs at farm tank level (random sampling once a month per producer) is the Brilliant Black- Reductase test (BRT-Test) which had been validated. The method detects beta-lactam antibiotics as well as other groups of antibiotics but the limit of detection is above the maximum residue limit for trimethoprim, lincomycin, sulfadimidine, gentamycin, erythromycin, tetracycline, oxytetracycline and cefquinome. 11

The tests used for testing of raw milk delivered to the dairies for residues of VMPs in the framework of the producers' own controls, was limited to beta-lactams in the dairies visited by the audit team, leaving other possibly used antibiotics undetected in raw milk. The rapid commercial tests were done either at truck and trailer level or truck compartment level by the driver. If the truck/trailer and/or compartment tested positive, the test was repeated as a confirmatory test using an automated reader and the result of this test was decisive.

A large dairy group was processing milk that had tested positive for residues of VMPs with the BRT test, and had used another commercial test for confirmation. The range of antibiotic residues with the second test did not cover all the types of beta-lactams that the first test did. This procedure had, in one dairy, led to 30 340 litres of milk that had tested positive in the first test but negative in the second test to be processed for human consumption in 2020-2022 (in total 49 cases). The FBOs opinion was this milk had been tested as false positive in the first test. The CAs in different Länder had accepted this approach.

The central and Land CAs do not have an oversight on how the raw milk quality control system is implemented: for first purchasers who receive 24 000 kg or less raw cow milk annually, milk producers in the agricultural sector who market their milk directly, farms that produce sheep and goat milk and first purchasers of sheep and goat milk.

The methods in place regarding testing of raw milk for antibiotic residues detects only a limited range of residues and the way the testing is implemented cannot guarantee that raw milk containing antibiotic residues is not entering into the production of dairy products for human consumption. 5.6 OFFICIAL CONTROLS OVER FOOD BUSINESS OPERATORS' COMPLIANCE WITH HYGIENE RULES Legal requirements Articles 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 137, 138 and 139 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls consistently check prescriptions of medicated feeds to de- termine their compliance with the relevant legal requirements. Legal basis: Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. Recommendation based on conclusion: 25. Associated finding: 21.
recommendations.legal_basis: Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. Recommendation based on conclusion: 25. Associated finding: 21.

citations.text: The Commission auditor scrutinised the documentation concerning manufacturing of medicated feed in the one establishment approved in Austria. In general, prescrip- tions, recipes and labels of medicated feed were available. However, the auditor not- ed that the reviewed prescriptions did not contain information on diagnosed disease to be treated, inclusion rate of active substances and any warnings necessary to en- sure the proper use. These information items are required to be included in the pre- scriptions by points 5, 8 and 13 of Annex V of Regulation (EU) 2019/4. The heading of the prescriptions reviewed referred to the repealed European legislation (which is no longer applicable) and did not contain the unique number required by point 2 of the above-mentioned Regulation. These deficiencies were overlooked during previ- ous official controls.

The Austrian competent authority has an adequate system in place to plan and imple- ment official inspections on manufacturing and placing on the market of medicated feed. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by the use of inappropriate prescriptions for the production of medicated feed. 6 OVERALL CONCLUSION In Austria, the competent authorities have put in place an adequate system to carry out official controls on feed business operators, including those manufacturing and placing on the market medicated feed. The actions taken by the competent authority to address (open) Recommendation 1 of the 2021 audit were effective and have led to a significant improvement in the official controls on feed business operators' HACCP based procedures. This recommendation can therefore be closed due to action taken. Whilst official inspections on manufacturing of medicated feed are regularly performed, they are not effective in verifying operator's procedures to comply with requirements on prescriptions, weakening an otherwise well-performing system. 7 CLOSING MEETING, A closing meeting was held on 11 October 2024 with representatives of the Austrian competent authorities. The auditor presented the main findings and preliminary conclusions of the audit. The competent authorities did not express any disagreement with those. 7 8 RECOMMENDATIONS The competent authorities are invited to provide details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion ('action plan'), aimed at addressing the recommendation set out below. With regard to those non-compliances noted in the audit report which did not result in a recommendation being made, the competent authorities are nevertheless, requested to address these. The effectiveness of actions taken to address such non-compliance will be assessed in future audits on this topic.
